question: My senior Lab keeps clearing his throat. Should I be worried?
answer: It's worth knowing about, because an occasional dry throat-clearing hack is the classic FIRST sign of laryngeal paralysis — and Labradors are about 70% of cases. It happens because the cartilage flaps at the top of the airway close a split second late when he swallows, so tiny droplets of saliva slip past and tickle the windpipe. It's most noticeable when eating, drinking, or resting in a dry room. Almost everyone files it under allergies, a hairball, or early heart disease — even cardiologists mistake it, because the sound is so similar. It genuinely might be allergies or dry air. But in a senior large-breed dog it's the one sign worth taking seriously early, because catching it early changes the whole trajectory.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: Did pulling on his collar cause my dog's laryngeal paralysis?
answer: No. Dr. Bryden Stanley, one of the leading GOLPP researchers, ran a study specifically on this question — comparing senior dogs WITH laryngeal paralysis against healthy dogs of the same age and breed, asking both groups about choke chains, spiked collars, and how hard the dog pulled on the leash. They found no difference between the groups. She has stated she has never seen laryngeal paralysis caused by a dog pulling on a collar. The only neck trauma that causes it is severe physical injury — a dog mauled or badly bitten in the throat, or a car accident. Not leash pulling, and not grabbing a collar to break up a scuffle. Switch to a harness going forward, but not out of blame — just because a compromised airway shouldn't have pressure on it.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: What is GOLPP and how is it different from laryngeal paralysis?
answer: They're the same thing seen at two zoom levels. Laryngeal paralysis is the visible symptom: the cartilage flaps at the top of the airway stop opening properly. GOLPP — Geriatric Onset Laryngeal Paralysis Polyneuropathy — is the disease behind it, and the acquired form was renamed around 2014 when research showed it isn't a local throat problem at all. It's a slow, generalised nerve disease. The longest nerves in the body fail first, and the nerve running to the larynx is one of the longest there is. So the throat is simply where a whole-body condition announces itself first, and the hind-end weakness that follows later is the same disease reaching shorter nerves.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: Does all laryngeal paralysis mean GOLPP?
answer: No, but in a senior large-breed dog, acquired laryngeal paralysis is almost always GOLPP. The other causes are specific and distinguishable. Congenital laryngeal paralysis is a hereditary defect that shows up in puppies under a year old — a completely different disease. A tumour can cause it: a thyroid mass in the neck or a chest tumour physically compressing the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which is why a CT is sometimes done. And direct trauma — a severe bite wound to the neck or a car accident — can sever the nerve. Once those are ruled out in an older dog, vets classify it as the acquired form, which is GOLPP.

question: My dog struggles in the heat on land but is completely fine swimming in 90-degree weather. Why?
answer: There's a clean anatomical reason, and that specific split is actually a meaningful clue. On land, dogs cool almost entirely by panting — and panting requires those laryngeal flaps to pull wide open to move air fast. If they can't dilate properly, panting becomes inefficient: he works harder, heats up faster, gets anxious, and the throat tissue swells, making it harder still. In water, none of that applies. He cools by conduction through his skin and belly, so his core temperature stays down without panting at all. That's why a dog can be miserable at 80°F on a field and completely happy at 90°F in a pool. It also means swimming is one of the best things you can give him.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: Is it safe to let a dog with laryngeal paralysis swim?
answer: Not only safe — it's among the best exercise available to him, with one hard rule. Swimming and wading are low-impact, build the hind-end muscle that GOLPP slowly takes, and cool him through the skin so he never has to pant heavily. The rule is NO DIVING: not off docks, not down after a sinking toy. His laryngeal flaps can't close to keep water out of his airway. Use floating toys he can grab from the surface, and keep a harness or life jacket on him. If you've been swimming your dog and now feel guilty about it, don't — that was the right call all along.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: What are the early warning signs of laryngeal paralysis in dogs?
answer: In roughly the order they appear. An occasional dry throat-clearing hack — the earliest and most-missed sign, worst when eating, drinking, or in a dry room. A changed bark: raspy, croaky, higher-pitched or lost, which about 50% of dogs get. Noise on the INHALE — a raspy or whistling stridor, often only when excited at first. Belly breathing: using stomach muscles to force air in, or panting heavily at rest. Heat intolerance that wasn't there last summer. And later, hind-end signs: toe drag, back claws wearing down, wavy back legs, thinning thighs. The critical caveat is that a normal bark rules out nothing — half of affected dogs never change their voice.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: My dog's bark sounds totally normal. Does that mean he doesn't have laryngeal paralysis?
answer: No — and this trips up a lot of owners. Only about 50% of dogs with laryngeal paralysis ever experience a change in their bark. The other half keep a completely normal voice throughout. A changed bark is a strong signal when it's present, because the vocal cords sit inside the larynx, but its absence is not evidence against the diagnosis. The signs that matter more are the occasional throat-clearing hack, noise on the inhale, and a new inability to handle heat.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: How is laryngeal paralysis diagnosed?
answer: With a laryngoscopy — the vet looks directly down the throat while the dog is under a very light plane of anaesthesia, usually with a respiratory stimulant like doxapram to force deep breaths, and watches whether the cartilages actually move or sit paralysed. Light sedation matters: too deep and normal cartilages stop moving too, which can produce a false positive. A CT is sometimes added to rule out a chest or thyroid tumour pressing on the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Worth knowing: even if you don't want the sedated exam, a basic vet consult is still valuable just to get rescue sedatives on hand for a breathing crisis.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: How fast does GOLPP progress?
answer: Slowly. The word the literature uses is insidious — it moves over months and years, not days or weeks. Many dogs live a long time with only noisy breathing when excited or on walks. The hind-end weakness typically becomes noticeable a year or two AFTER the respiratory signs start, and only about 29% of dogs show any visible weakness at the time the airway problem is diagnosed. For a real-world example: Dr. Mary Gardner's Doberman Duncan started clearing his throat at 10, was diagnosed then, lived nearly three more years, and died at 13 of an unrelated heart condition — not of GOLPP. And Dobermans have a shorter lifespan than Labradors.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: Will my dog eventually lose the use of his back legs?
answer: Because GOLPP is systemic, virtually all dogs develop some degree of hind-limb weakness if they live long enough — but it is gradual, and critically, it is NOT painful. It's nerve signal loss, not arthritis. It starts as a subtle toe drag: the middle back claws wearing down, a light scritch on pavement. Then loss of proprioception, so the back legs look wavy when standing. Then thinning muscle in the thighs and glutes. This does not mean sudden paralysis. Most GOLPP dogs stay mobile and happy for the rest of their lives with simple help — yoga mats or runners over slippery floors, and a double-handled support harness for stairs and getting up.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: Can my dog still play fetch and run if he has laryngeal paralysis?
answer: Yes, with modifications — the danger is heat, not the running itself. Never play fetch on a hot field or in humid weather, because he can't cool himself efficiently and the overheating cascade is what closes airways. Move the high-energy version to water: he can chase floating toys in a pool or ocean and stay cool the whole time, as long as he doesn't dive under. On land, keep sessions short, low, and on cool days or early mornings, and stop before he starts panting heavily. Keep throws low so he isn't leaping, which is hard on senior joints anyway. Formal high-level athletics usually get retired, but backyard fun and swimming carry on for years.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: What can I do at home to slow down GOLPP?
answer: More than you'd think, and most of it is free. Strict temperature control is the single biggest one — air conditioning, a fan by his bed, never exercise in heat, because overheating triggers a throat-swelling cascade. Retire the collar for a harness so nothing presses on a compromised airway. Keep him lean: extra weight is extra work for a restricted respiratory system and extra load on weakening hind legs. Manage excitement and anxiety, not just exercise, since heavy panting makes the tissues slam together and swell. Slow his water down so he doesn't gulp and inhale it. Run a cool-mist humidifier in the bedroom, and get rid of plug-ins, incense, potpourri, scented dryer sheets and smoke.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: Should I use a slow feeder for a dog with laryngeal paralysis?
answer: For water yes, for food probably not — and this one is genuinely counterintuitive. Swallowing studies found that a LARGER mouthful of food works better for these dogs: a big bolus physically stretches the oesophagus, which triggers a stronger and more coordinated swallowing wave. Tiny slow bites can actually make swallowing more sluggish. So the slow feeder that's right for water may be working against him at mealtimes. Water is the opposite — gulping a whole bowl is a major trigger for inhaling water and regurgitating, so small frequent amounts or a floating bowl that limits flow is right there. If dry food dust makes him cough, moisten it. Watch how he actually does and let that decide.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: Do elevated bowls help a dog with laryngeal paralysis?
answer: Standard shoulder-height elevated bowls show no clinical benefit for GOLPP dogs. What does help about 50% of them is feeding on an INCLINE — on stairs, or holding the bowl so his head sits significantly higher than his stomach, using gravity to carry the food down. It's worth experimenting: some GOLPP dogs genuinely do better on the ground, others clearly do better on an incline. Try both for a week each and watch which produces less hacking after meals.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: What natural remedies help laryngeal paralysis?
answer: Several, aimed at three targets — the cough, the swelling, and the anxiety. Honey is the simplest and most effective for the hack itself, at half to one teaspoon per 10 lb twice daily; it coats an irritated throat and suppresses coughing naturally. CBD oil at 3 mg per 10 lb once or twice daily breaks the panic loop where restriction causes anxiety causes faster breathing causes more swelling. Curcumin at 95% extract, 100 mg per 10 lb, with boswellia at 50 mg per 10 lb, are anti-inflammatories for laryngeal swelling. Licorice root tincture at 1 mL per 40 lb twice daily acts as a natural corticosteroid and cough suppressant — but maximum 14 days, then a 7-day break. Green tea extract at 200–400 mg daily for a Lab-sized dog is used for its immune-modulating effect on nerve degeneration.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: How much honey can I give my dog for coughing?
answer: Half to one teaspoon per 10 lb of body weight, twice daily. For a 75 lb Lab that's roughly 4 to 7 teaspoons per dose. It's one of the simplest and most effective things available for a throat-clearing hack — it coats irritated tissue and naturally suppresses coughing. Most dogs, retrievers especially, will lick it straight off a spoon, or you can stir it into food. Using local raw honey may help with seasonal allergies as a side benefit. It's cheap, safe, and worth trying before anything more complicated.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: Why does licorice root have to be limited to 14 days?
answer: Because it works like a corticosteroid, and that's exactly why it needs a break. Licorice root is a genuinely effective anti-inflammatory and cough suppressant with immune-modulating properties, dosed at 1 mL of tincture per 40 lb twice daily. But it affects cortisol and potassium levels, so the protocol is a maximum of 14 days followed by a 7-day break before restarting. It isn't a permanent daily supplement the way honey or omega-3 can be. If your dog needs continuous suppression to be comfortable, that's information — it means the underlying inflammation needs addressing rather than more bandaging.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: What physical therapy helps a dog with GOLPP hind-end weakness?
answer: Four things, and they're all doable at home. Cavaletti poles — low poles or broomsticks an inch or two off the ground that he steps over slowly. GOLPP dogs lose proprioception, the brain's automatic sense of where the paws are, so stepping over poles forces him to look at his feet and place them consciously, exercising exactly the pathway that's fading. Sit-to-stands and side-steps are squats for dogs, keeping the glutes and thighs from wasting. Swimming and wading are the best of the lot: low-impact, strength-building and cooling, with no diving. And traction — yoga mats or runners over hardwood, because slippery floors are what turn mild weakness into a dog who won't get up. Electroacupuncture is the most-recommended professional addition.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: What is electroacupuncture and does it help laryngeal paralysis?
answer: It's acupuncture with a tiny electrical current run through the needles, and it's the most-recommended holistic modality for GOLPP. The current stimulates the damaged nerves to fire, which in turn contracts and exercises the muscles those nerves serve — used for both the larynx itself and the weakening hind end. Clinical reports from GOLPP-focused vets describe it as one of the most effective non-surgical ways to keep those pathways active. Formal research interest is active but some studies were cut short, so the evidence base is clinical rather than trial-grade. It's non-invasive and worth asking an integrative vet about.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: Can I manage laryngeal paralysis without surgery?
answer: Yes, and many owners do it successfully for years. For stable, mildly affected dogs, vets routinely recommend medical and lifestyle management first before surgery is even discussed. The tie-back procedure exists and works, but it isn't the only path and it isn't urgent for a dog with mild signs. If surgery isn't financially possible right now, that is not a failure — the management is what they'd tell you to do anyway: strict temperature control, harness instead of collar, lean weight, slow water, moist air, and calm surroundings. The one thing worth a vet visit regardless is getting rescue sedatives on hand.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: Why do I need sedatives on hand for a dog with laryngeal paralysis?
answer: Because a breathing crisis is a feedback loop, and a sedative breaks it. If your dog gets overheated, excited or anxious, his breathing speeds up — which makes the laryngeal tissues slam together, swell, and restrict the airway further, which increases the panic. Given at the very first sign of panic-breathing, a vet-prescribed sedative like acepromazine, trazodone or gabapentin calms the nervous system, slows the breathing, and prevents the swelling cascade. It turns what would be a high-stress emergency-room night into something you can stabilise at home. Having it in the cupboard is one of the highest-value things a vet visit gets you, even if you never pursue surgery.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: Why does my dog hack more at night in my bedroom?
answer: Almost certainly dry air. Air conditioning and forced heating strip moisture out of indoor air, and the larynx is highly sensitive to it — dry tissue triggers exactly that sudden, dry tickle-hack. It's one of the most common patterns owners describe: fine all day, hacking in the bedroom at night. A cool-mist humidifier or vaporiser in that room is one of the cheapest and most effective fixes available. While you're at it, remove the other airway irritants: chemical plug-ins, incense, potpourri, scented dryer sheets and any smoke.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: Is there real research behind the natural remedies for GOLPP?
answer: Honest answer: not specifically. There are no large controlled trials of curcumin, licorice root or EGCG in dogs with GOLPP. The condition was only identified as a systemic disease around 2014, and most research funding since has gone to genetics, surgical tie-back outcomes and physical rehabilitation. The doses used come from clinical experience and the established pharmacology of each compound, applied by integrative veterinarians. Electroacupuncture has the most active clinical interest of the group, though some formal studies were cut short. That doesn't make these useless — they're low-risk, symptom-directed, and widely used — but it's worth knowing the evidence is clinical rather than trial-grade.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP

question: What breeds get GOLPP and at what age?
answer: Senior large breeds, overwhelmingly. Labrador Retrievers are about 70% of cases, followed by Golden Retrievers, Dobermans, Newfoundlands, Rottweilers and Great Pyrenees. The average age at diagnosis is 11.3 years, and it's three to four times more common in male dogs. It can absolutely present earlier — vets diagnose it at 8 fairly regularly, and the youngest documented cases are around 6. So an 8-year-old Lab with an occasional hack is on the young side of typical but well within range, and being on the younger side with no hind-end weakness yet is a genuinely favourable starting position.
source: Common Sense Dog — laryngeal paralysis & GOLPP
